Kyrgyzstan targets up to 39% emission cut by 2035

Kyrgyzstan has unveiled its updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0), outlining an ambitious plan to cut net greenhouse gas emissions by up to 30% by 2030 and 39% by 2035 with international support, while promoting a just, inclusive, and green transition aligned with the Paris Agreement and national development goals.

13 October 2025, 15:003 min read735 views0 comments0

By 2030, Kyrgyzstan aims to cut its net greenhouse gas emissions by 18% from baseline levels — or up to 30% with international support. By 2035, the target rises to 16% (and up to 39% with external assistance). These measures are expected to reduce annual emissions by 8.5mn tons of CO₂ equivalent by 2030 and 13.1mn tons by 2035.

The targets form the core of Kyrgyzstan’s newly presented Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) — a comprehensive roadmap outlining how the country will reduce emissions and adapt to climate change through 2035.

Fully aligned with the Paris Agreement, the National Development Programme 2030, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), NDC 3.0 reflects Kyrgyzstan’s ambition to balance climate responsibility with economic growth. Although the country accounts for less than 0.034% of global emissions, it faces disproportionate climate impacts, from glacial retreat to water scarcity and land degradation.

“The development and approval of Kyrgyzstan’s new NDC 3.0 is another indicator of our responsible and active role in international policy, and our readiness to take on greater commitments in addressing the consequences of global climate change,” said Edil Baisalov, Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers. “At COP30, we will call on developed countries to bear their share of responsibility for climate pollution. Kyrgyzstan has a full right to development. The question is how to adapt our economy and way of life to a changing world.”

Meder Mashiev, Minister of Natural Resources, Ecology, and Technical Supervision, emphasized that Kyrgyzstan stands for climate justice and equal access to financing and technologies for mountain countries.

“We believe that the green transition is not a threat but an opportunity for a new economy, new jobs, and a decent future for our citizens,” Mashiev said.

Antje Grawe, UN Resident Coordinator in Kyrgyzstan, noted that NDC 3.0 puts people at the center of the transition.

“A low-carbon transition can only succeed if it is just and inclusive. This approach ensures that climate action supports livelihoods and social cohesion while driving sustainable economic transformation,” she said.

The new plan establishes a framework for investments in clean energy, energy-efficient buildings and industries, climate-smart agriculture, and sustainable urban infrastructure. These measures are designed to boost productivity, create export opportunities, and generate employment.

UNDP Resident Representative Alexandra Solovieva added that the updated NDC “opens new opportunities for growth,” noting that “energy efficiency becomes a tool for cost reduction and competitiveness, renewable energy strengthens independence, and green industry and waste management create new jobs and innovations.”

A key feature of NDC 3.0 is the principle of a just transition, ensuring that workers and communities are supported during the shift toward a green economy. The plan also expands on social inclusion, addressing education, gender equality, youth engagement, and social protection.

To meet its goals, Kyrgyzstan will rely on international climate finance — mobilizing concessional funding from donors, financial institutions, and impact investors. The NDC serves as a blueprint for attracting such investments, linking climate action to long-term economic transformation.

Developed with technical support from UNDP and UN agencies, NDC 3.0 involved input from over 1,000 participants, including government bodies, civil society, business leaders, and youth representatives. The outcomes of this inclusive process were consolidated during the National Climate Dialogue in Bishkek.

Kyrgyzstan will present its updated climate commitments at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP30) in Brazil, where countries are expected to outline concrete steps to keep global warming below 1.5°C and accelerate global climate finance.
